questions.explanation_en: A worm replicates itself and spreads across networks on its own, without attaching to a host file; the description given fits a virus, which needs a host program and usually a user action. The other three pairings are correct.

questions.chapter: Networks — Network Security, Internet & Web Basics
questions.question_en:
Consider the following statements:
I. A substitution cipher replaces each letter with another letter or symbol.
II. A transposition cipher changes the positions of the letters but keeps the letters themselves.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.explanation_en: Both are correct. A substitution cipher (for example Caesar or Vigenère) disguises letters by replacing them, while a transposition cipher (for example rail-fence or columnar) only reorders them, so its ciphertext keeps the same letter frequencies as the plaintext.

questions.chapter: Networks — Network Security, Internet & Web Basics
questions.question_en: Using a Caesar cipher with a shift of 3 (A→D), what is the ciphertext for the plaintext NETWORK?
questions.explanation_en: Shift each letter forward by 3: N→Q, E→H, T→W, W→Z, O→R, R→U, K→N, giving QHWZRUN. KBQTLOH is a backward shift of 3 (which is decryption), and RIXASVO uses a shift of 4.

questions.chapter: Networks — Network Security, Internet & Web Basics
questions.question_en: Which group contains ONLY asymmetric (public-key) algorithms?
questions.explanation_en: RSA, Diffie–Hellman, ECC (elliptic-curve cryptography) and DSA all use a public/private key pair. AES, DES, 3DES, IDEA, RC4 and Blowfish are symmetric — the same secret key encrypts and decrypts — so any group containing one of them is wrong.

questions.chapter: Networks — Network Security, Internet & Web Basics
questions.question_en: Which algorithm–key-length pairing is correct?
questions.explanation_en: AES (Rijndael) uses a 128-bit block with 128-, 192- or 256-bit keys (10, 12 or 14 rounds). DES has a 56-bit effective key (64 bits including parity), IDEA uses a 128-bit key, and Blowfish takes a variable key of 32 to 448 bits.

questions.chapter: Networks — Network Security, Internet & Web Basics
questions.question_en: Triple DES with three independent keys uses a total key length of ___ bits, but because of the meet-in-the-middle attack it offers effective security of about ___ bits.
questions.explanation_en: Each DES key is 56 bits, so three keys give 3 × 56 = 168 bits. A meet-in-the-middle attack reduces the effective strength to about 2 × 56 = 112 bits. '112; 56' describes the two-key version's key length and single DES's strength, not three-key 3DES.

questions.chapter: Networks — Network Security, Internet & Web Basics
questions.question_en: Ten users want every pair among them to be able to communicate secretly. How many keys are needed with symmetric-key cryptography, and how many with public-key cryptography?
questions.explanation_en: Symmetric: one shared key per pair = n(n − 1)/2 = 10 × 9 / 2 = 45 keys. Public-key: each user needs one key pair, so 2n = 20 keys (10 public + 10 private). '45 and 10' counts only the public keys.

questions.chapter: Networks — Network Security, Internet & Web Basics
questions.question_en: In protocols such as TLS, the bulk data is encrypted with ___, while ___ is used to exchange it securely.

options.en: the receiver's private key; a hash function such as SHA-256
a temporary symmetric session key; public-key cryptography
a long-term public key; a symmetric stream cipher like RC4
a message digest; a certificate revocation list from the CA

questions.explanation_en: Symmetric ciphers such as AES are fast, so a fresh session key is created for one session and used for the bulk data; slower public-key methods (RSA or Diffie–Hellman) are used only to agree on or carry that key. Encrypting all data directly with a public-key algorithm would be far too slow.

questions.chapter: Networks — Network Security, Internet & Web Basics
questions.question_en: The message digests produced by MD5 and SHA-1 are, respectively:
questions.explanation_en: MD5 produces a 128-bit digest and SHA-1 a 160-bit digest, while SHA-256 (SHA-2 family) produces 256 bits. MD5 and SHA-1 are now considered broken for collision resistance, so SHA-256 or stronger is recommended.

questions.chapter: Networks — Network Security, Internet & Web Basics
questions.question_en: To create a digital signature the sender uses ___, and the receiver verifies it with ___.

options.en: the sender's public key; the sender's private key
the receiver's public key; the receiver's private key
a shared secret key; the same shared secret key
the sender's private key; the sender's public key

questions.explanation_en: The sender signs (encrypts the message hash) with its own private key, which only it holds, and anyone can verify the signature with the sender's public key; this gives authentication, integrity and non-repudiation. Encrypting with the receiver's public key provides confidentiality, not a signature.

questions.chapter: Networks — Network Security, Internet & Web Basics
questions.question_en: When a browser opens an HTTPS site, how does the server prove that its public key really belongs to it?

options.en: By sending its private key to the browser for checking
By using port 443, which only genuine servers may use
By presenting a digital certificate signed by a trusted CA
By sending an MD5 hash of its home page to the browser

questions.explanation_en: HTTPS is HTTP over SSL/TLS (port 443). During the TLS handshake the server sends an X.509 certificate that binds its domain name to its public key and is signed by a Certificate Authority the browser trusts. A private key is never sent to anyone, and a port number proves nothing about identity.

questions.chapter: Networks — Network Security, Internet & Web Basics
questions.question_en: IPsec works at the ___ layer, and its ___ mode, which encrypts the whole original IP packet, is used for site-to-site VPNs.
questions.explanation_en: IPsec protects IP packets at the network layer using AH (authentication) and ESP (encryption). Tunnel mode wraps the entire original packet inside a new IP header, as VPN gateways do; transport mode protects only the payload and keeps the original header, so it suits host-to-host links.

questions.chapter: Networks — Network Security, Internet & Web Basics
questions.question_en: In network security, a DMZ is:

options.en: A firewall that checks only source and destination IP addresses
An attack that floods a server until it can no longer respond
A protocol that encrypts traffic between a browser and a server
A separate subnet for public servers between the LAN and the Internet

questions.explanation_en: A demilitarised zone (perimeter network) holds Internet-facing servers such as web and mail servers, so outsiders can reach them while firewalls still shield the internal LAN. A firewall that checks only addresses and ports is a packet-filtering firewall; stateful firewalls also track connection state, and proxy firewalls inspect application content.

questions.chapter: Networks — Network Security, Internet & Web Basics
questions.question_en: Which statement correctly distinguishes an IDS from an IPS?

options.en: An IDS blocks attacks inline; an IPS only logs and raises alerts
An IDS detects and alerts; an IPS sits inline and blocks attacks
An IDS encrypts the traffic; an IPS decrypts it at the receiver
An IDS works only on hosts; an IPS works only on the Internet

questions.explanation_en: An Intrusion Detection System watches a copy of the traffic (or host logs), matches signatures or anomalies and raises alerts, but does not stop the traffic. An Intrusion Prevention System is placed inline, so it can drop malicious packets or reset connections in real time. Swapping the two roles is the common trap.

questions.chapter: Networks — Network Security, Internet & Web Basics
questions.question_en: ARPANET, the forerunner of the Internet, was:

options.en: A circuit-switched telephone network built by AT&T in 1975
An early packet-switched network, funded by the US DoD in 1969
The first web browser, developed at CERN in the year 1990
The backbone network that NSF built for universities in 1986

questions.explanation_en: ARPANET was funded by ARPA of the US Department of Defense and first linked four nodes (UCLA, SRI, UCSB and the University of Utah) in 1969 using packet switching (it was the first wide-area packet-switched network); it switched to TCP/IP on 1 January 1983. NSFNET (1986) was a later backbone that took over ARPANET's role.

questions.chapter: Networks — Network Security, Internet & Web Basics
questions.question_en: The World Wide Web was proposed in 1989 by:
questions.explanation_en: Tim Berners-Lee proposed the WWW at CERN in 1989 and created HTTP, HTML, URLs, the first web server and the first browser. Vint Cerf, with Bob Kahn, designed TCP/IP and is called a 'father of the Internet', which makes him the usual distractor; Tomlinson sent the first network e-mail and Andreessen built the Mosaic browser.

questions.chapter: Networks — Network Security, Internet & Web Basics
questions.question_en:
Consider the following statements:
I. The World Wide Web is a service that runs on top of the Internet.
II. E-mail and FTP are parts of the World Wide Web.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.explanation_en: Only I is correct. The Internet is the global network of networks running TCP/IP; the WWW is one service on it — linked hypertext pages fetched with HTTP. E-mail (SMTP, POP3, IMAP) and FTP are separate Internet services, not parts of the Web.

questions.chapter: Networks — Network Security, Internet & Web Basics
questions.question_en: In the URL https://www.example.org:8443/docs/index.html, what does '8443' represent?
questions.explanation_en: A URL has the form protocol://host:port/path. Here https is the protocol (scheme), www.example.org is the host or domain name, 8443 is the port number (replacing the default 443) and /docs/index.html is the path. Without ':8443' the browser would use port 443 for HTTPS.

questions.chapter: Networks — Network Security, Internet & Web Basics
questions.question_en: Mozilla Firefox, Google Search and Apache HTTP Server are, respectively, examples of:

options.en: a browser, a search engine and a web server
a search engine, a browser and a web server
a web server, a search engine and a browser
a browser, a web server and a search engine

questions.explanation_en: A browser (Firefox, Chrome) is client software that requests and displays web pages; a search engine (Google Search, Bing) is a website that indexes pages and finds them by keyword; a web server (Apache, Nginx, IIS) stores pages and serves them over HTTP. Mixing up a search engine with a browser is the classic error.

questions.chapter: Networks — Network Security, Internet & Web Basics
questions.question_en: Moving from one web page to another by following hyperlinks, often without a fixed goal, is commonly called:
questions.explanation_en: Web surfing (browsing) is a person moving through websites by clicking links. Web crawling is done by search-engine bots that visit pages automatically to index them, and web hosting means storing a website on a server so that others can reach it.

questions.chapter: Networks — Network Security, Internet & Web Basics
questions.question_en: Which broadband Internet connection uses existing telephone lines and lets voice calls and data share the line at the same time?
questions.explanation_en: DSL (for example ADSL) carries data over the copper telephone line at frequencies above the voice band, so the phone still works while the user is connected to the ISP. Dial-up also uses the phone line but occupies it completely and is limited to 56 kbps; cable broadband uses the TV coaxial network.

questions.chapter: Networks — Network Security, Internet & Web Basics
questions.question_en: When an e-mail is sent with some addresses in the BCC field:

options.en: BCC recipients are hidden from all other recipients
BCC recipients are not allowed to reply to the sender
BCC recipients receive only the subject of the e-mail
BCC recipients are shown to everyone in the To field

questions.explanation_en: BCC (blind carbon copy) recipients get the full message, but their addresses are not shown to the To, CC or other BCC recipients. CC (carbon copy) recipients, by contrast, are visible to everyone who receives the mail.

questions.chapter: Networks — Network Security, Internet & Web Basics
questions.question_en: A web cookie is:

options.en: A program a website installs to scan the user's files
A small piece of data a website stores in the user's browser
A temporary copy of a whole web page kept on the server
A key the browser uses to encrypt all HTTPS traffic

questions.explanation_en: A cookie is a small text record (a name–value pair) that a server sends with Set-Cookie and the browser returns on later requests, letting sites remember logins, carts and preferences. It is passive data, not a program, so it cannot scan files; third-party cookies are the ones used for cross-site tracking.

questions.chapter: Networks — Mobile & Wireless Communication
questions.question_en: Which statement about GSM's HLR and VLR is correct?

options.en: HLR holds permanent subscriber data; VLR holds temporary data of visitors in its area
VLR holds permanent subscriber data; HLR holds temporary data of visitors in its area
HLR and VLR both store only the IMEI numbers of stolen or blocked handsets
HLR is located inside each BTS, while VLR is located inside each BSC

questions.explanation_en: The HLR is the home operator's central database with each subscriber's permanent profile (IMSI, services, current location area). The VLR, usually co-located with an MSC, keeps temporary copies for subscribers currently in its area and informs the HLR when a mobile registers there. IMEIs of stolen handsets are kept in the EIR.

questions.chapter: Networks — Mobile & Wireless Communication
questions.question_en: Which GSM element–function pairing is INCORRECT?

options.en: BSC – controls a group of BTSs and their radio channels
EIR – stores the permanent profile of every subscriber
MSC – switches calls and connects to other networks
AuC – holds the secret keys used for authentication

questions.explanation_en: The EIR (Equipment Identity Register) keeps IMEI numbers in white, grey and black lists to block stolen or faulty handsets; permanent subscriber profiles are stored in the HLR. The other pairings are correct: BTS and BSC form the Base Station Subsystem, the MSC does switching, and the AuC holds the key Ki for authentication and ciphering.

questions.chapter: Networks — Mobile & Wireless Communication
questions.question_en: Which generation–technology pairing is INCORRECT?

options.en: 2G – GSM with digital voice and SMS
5G – first generation to use digital transmission

questions.explanation_en: Digital transmission began with 2G (GSM, 1991); 1G systems such as AMPS carried analog voice only. 3G (UMTS/WCDMA, CDMA2000) brought mobile broadband, 4G (LTE and LTE-Advanced) is all-IP, and 5G adds very high data rates, about 1 ms latency and support for massive IoT.

questions.chapter: Networks — Mobile & Wireless Communication
questions.question_en: A soft handover, typical of CDMA systems, is one in which:

options.en: The mobile leaves the old cell before joining the new one
The call moves between channels of the same base station
The mobile joins the new cell before leaving the old one
The call is dropped and must be redialled in the new cell

questions.explanation_en: Soft handover is make-before-break: during the transition the mobile is linked to two or more base stations at once, which CDMA allows because neighbouring cells use the same frequency. Break-before-make is hard handover, used in GSM (FDMA/TDMA).

questions.chapter: Networks — Mobile & Wireless Communication
questions.question_en: In a satellite system, transferring a call from one spot beam to another spot beam of the same satellite is called:
questions.explanation_en: Schiller lists four satellite handovers: intra-satellite (between spot beams of one satellite), inter-satellite (between two satellites), gateway (the satellite changes its ground gateway) and inter-system (between a satellite network and a terrestrial cellular network). Inter-satellite handover involves two different satellites, not two beams of the same one.

questions.chapter: Networks — Mobile & Wireless Communication
questions.question_en: In Mobile IP, if the mobile node obtains a temporary address itself, for example through DHCP, and acts as its own tunnel endpoint, that address is called the:
questions.explanation_en: The care-of address (COA) is the current tunnel endpoint for the mobile node. With a co-located COA the mobile node gets the address itself (for example via DHCP) and de-capsulates packets itself; with a foreign-agent COA the tunnel ends at the FA's address. The FA is a router, not an address — the 2023 official key that gave 'FA' for the DHCP-obtained tunnel endpoint was wrong; the correct answer is the COA.

questions.chapter: Networks — Mobile & Wireless Communication
questions.question_en: In Mobile IP, packets that a correspondent node sends to the mobile node's home address are intercepted by the ___ and tunnelled to the ___.
questions.explanation_en: The home agent, a router on the home network, intercepts datagrams addressed to the mobile node's permanent home address, encapsulates them (IP-in-IP) and tunnels them to the current care-of address. The foreign agent, if one is used, de-tunnels and delivers them; replies from the mobile node can go straight to the correspondent node (triangular routing).

questions.chapter: Networks — Mobile & Wireless Communication
questions.question_en: Which satellite orbit gives the lowest propagation delay but needs a large constellation of satellites for continuous global coverage?
questions.explanation_en: Low Earth Orbit satellites are close to the Earth, so the ground-to-satellite-to-ground delay is only about 5–10 ms, but each covers a small footprint and moves fast, so dozens or even thousands are needed (Iridium, Starlink). GEO satellites appear stationary and three can cover most of the Earth, but their ground-to-satellite-to-ground delay is about 250 ms (about 0.5 s for a question and its reply).

questions.chapter: Networks — Mobile & Wireless Communication
questions.question_en: A laptop used on a Wi-Fi network while travelling in a train belongs to which category of mobile computing devices?
questions.explanation_en: Schiller's four categories are fixed and wired (a desktop PC), mobile and wired (a laptop plugged into the network at each place), fixed and wireless (for example desktop PCs on a wireless LAN in a historic building where cabling is not allowed) and mobile and wireless (a device used on the move without cables). A laptop on Wi-Fi in a moving train is mobile and wireless.

questions.chapter: Networks — Mobile & Wireless Communication
questions.question_en: The IEEE standards for Wi-Fi, Bluetooth and WiMAX are, respectively:
questions.explanation_en: Wi-Fi wireless LANs follow IEEE 802.11 (a/b/g/n/ac/ax), Bluetooth was standardised as IEEE 802.15.1 (a WPAN) and WiMAX (broadband wireless MAN) is IEEE 802.16. 802.3 is wired Ethernet and 802.15.4 is the low-rate WPAN standard used by Zigbee.

tests.description: Every most expected Networks question in one timed test (−0.25 per wrong answer).
